messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Six months ago, Silas Cole, a 68-year-old widowed African American policy analyst, collapsed behind his mahogany desk during a quarterly fiscal review. A sudden, vise-like pressure seized his chest, and the hum of the D.C. building faded into a terrifying rush of blood. Paramedics found him unresponsive from a massive arrhythmia. The subsequent weeks in the intensive care unit were a blur of gasping through a plastic tube and the cold, clinical certainty that he would not wake up. He survived the episode, but the narrow escape permanently anchored his worldview to the fear of his own physiology. Now, Silas navigates his daily routine with a grim, rigid focus that leaves no room for the dense policy briefs demanding his attention. His body remains constantly tense, a coiled spring waiting to react to danger. Even inside his own home, he feels on guard, pacing the hallway each evening to check the deadbolts and listen for the unnatural creak of settling floorboards. When the conference room vents shudder to life with a low mechanical whine, his breath catches, and he instinctively shifts his posture toward the heavy oak door. He has learned to sit near the office exit, his shoulders locked, convinced that another collapse is merely hours away. He stares at columns of fiscal data until the numbers blur, fully aware that he has lost the ability to concentrate on anything but the quiet dread of impending failure. The past refuses to stay buried, and Silas’s relationship with his recollections has shifted into something alien. When the memory of the ICU returns, he can recall the clinical details perfectly, yet he feels completely numb, as if he is watching a stranger endure those final, fragile hours. The recollection arrives with such visceral immediacy that it feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over. When the sensation peaks, the sheer weight of emotion forces him to stop what he is doing and push his chair back, his chest heaving. This sudden surge of physiological arousal immediately triggers his threat response; the moment the image forms, his muscles clamp down and his heart drums against his ribs, turning the office into a hostile territory where concentration becomes impossible. Silas had come to believe he would never be able to feel normal emotions again, viewing his own physiology as an enemy that keeps reacting as if he is still in danger even when he is safe. Because he can no longer trust his own body, he scans his environment with exhausted vigilance, ensuring his threat response never fully disengages. Yet this constant state of hypervigilance becomes a catalyst for the very thing he dreads: a sudden lurch in his stomach or a tightness in his jaw instantly pulls him back into the ICU memories, which in turn flood him with terror that he is still dying. The more he tries to suppress the panic, the more certain he becomes that his mind and body are permanently fractured. He knows he can no longer trust himself to navigate a simple board meeting without the fear of collapsing overtaking his judgment, a realization that has quietly eroded his standing among his former colleagues. The breaking point arrived when he could no longer sit through a senior leadership briefing without fleeing the room, his hands shaking and his breath shallow. He has scheduled his first consultation with a trauma specialist, hoping to silence the internal alarm that has haunted him since that day behind his desk. Most of all, what frightened him most was the thought that he would never find peace with his own heartbeat, though he desperately hopes to reclaim the ability to simply exist without bracing for the end.
